result: Large-scale GWAS studies have identified hundreds of SNPs associated with educational attainment. While individual SNPs have very small effects (median 1.7 weeks of schooling), polygenic scores combining all SNPs explain up to 13% of variance in years of education and 9.2% in educational achievement (GPA).
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 accurately report findings from published GWAS studies (Lee et al., 2018) with appropriate citations. The claims correctly distinguish between individual SNP effects and combined polygenic score performance, providing specific quantitative estimates with proper context.

result: At age 7, polygenic scores showed positive correlations with educational achievement and explained additional variance beyond age and sex alone. However, pupil characteristics (FSM, SEN, EFL status) outperformed polygenic scores, with combined models explaining up to 26.3% of variance when including parental social background. The incremental R² of polygenic scores over pupil characteristics was modest (1.8-4.8%).
evaluation: Claims C22-C29 present consistent findings from regression analyses with appropriate confidence intervals. The hierarchical modeling approach properly quantifies incremental variance explained, and the results are supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

result: At age 16, polygenic scores explained 3.4-12.9% additional variance beyond age and sex. However, parental education and socioeconomic position provided greater explanatory power (19-21.4% additional variance). Most importantly, prior achievement at age 14 explained 65.1% of variance, and conditional on prior achievement, polygenic scores provided virtually no additional predictive power.
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are well-supported by regression analyses with confidence intervals reported. The key finding that prior achievement dominates prediction is clearly demonstrated in Figure 2, showing polygenic scores add minimal incremental variance when prior achievement is available.

result: Distribution analyses revealed near-complete overlap in polygenic scores between high achievers (top 10%) and other pupils, suggesting high misclassification rates. In contrast, prior achievement distributions showed much less overlap between groups. Visual inspection of predictions confirmed substantial misclassification from polygenic scores, similar to parental socioeconomic measures but worse than prior attainment.
evaluation: Claims C34-C39 are supported by distribution plots in Figures 3-4 and supplements. The visual evidence clearly demonstrates the overlap issue, and the inference about misclassification logically follows from the observed distributions. The comparison across predictors is appropriately documented.

result: ROC curve analysis for age 7 achievement showed polygenic scores had lower discriminatory ability (AUC: 0.63-0.68) compared to parental socioeconomic measures (AUC: 0.70). The sensitivity-specificity trade-off was poor across all measures, requiring near-universal classification to capture most high achievers. Results were consistent across different achievement cut-offs.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 are supported by ROC analyses in Figure 5 with specific AUC values reported. The interpretation of poor sensitivity-specificity trade-offs is appropriate given the ROC curves. Sensitivity analyses (Figure 5 supplement 1) confirm robustness to definition of high achievers.

result: At age 16, prior achievement measures provided far superior discrimination (AUC: 0.83-0.95) compared to polygenic scores (AUC: 0.61-0.70). After accounting for phenotypic information available to schools, polygenic scores provided almost no discriminatory ability (AUC: 0.51-0.56). Results were consistent when using earlier prior achievement measures.
evaluation: Claims C44-C48 are well-supported by ROC analyses in Figure 6 and supplements. The residualization analysis (Figure 6c) appropriately tests incremental value, and the near-chance AUC values (0.51-0.56) clearly demonstrate lack of added predictive utility beyond available phenotypic data.

result: Practical classification analysis showed that selecting students by top 10% polygenic scores would only capture 24% of actual top achievers (76% false positives), while using age 11 phenotypic measures would capture 51%. This demonstrates that polygenic scores cannot identify high achievers more accurately than available phenotypic measures, despite group-level associations.
evaluation: Claims C49-C52 provide concrete quantification of classification accuracy that follows logically from the ROC analyses. The specific percentages illustrate the practical implications of the poor discriminatory ability, making the abstract AUC values interpretable for educational policy.

result: Summary of main findings: Polygenic scores explained 3.4-12.9% variance in achievement (higher than original GWAS), but prior achievement was the strongest predictor. Conditional on prior achievement, polygenic scores added minimal predictive power. Parental socioeconomic factors outperformed polygenic scores. Genetic data provided little incremental information over readily available phenotypic data, except when prior achievement is unavailable.
evaluation: Claims C53-C59 accurately summarize the study's main findings, appropriately synthesizing results from multiple analyses. The comparison to original GWAS (C54) is valid, and the conditional conclusions (C56-C57) correctly reflect the hierarchical modeling results. The overall inference is well-supported by the data.

result: The authors propose that lack of incremental genetic prediction may be because prior achievement mediates genetic effects. They note theoretical work suggesting 75% genetic variance explanation may be needed for individual prediction, and that their scores (from >1 million person GWAS) would require much larger samples to improve. However, even improved variance explanation may not provide useful returns for personalized interventions if genetic effects are phenotypically expressed.
evaluation: Claims C61-C69 are largely speculative (C61, C64, C66) or cite theoretical work (C63). While the mediation hypothesis (C61-C62) is plausible, it is not directly tested. The logical reasoning about requirements for actionable prediction (C67-C69) is sound, but these remain theoretical considerations rather than empirically demonstrated findings.

result: Individual-level predictions from polygenic scores and parental background were imprecise due to stochastic factors important at individual but not group level. While high polygenic scores associated with higher achievement on average, genetics did not determine outcomes. Achievement results from combinations of genetic factors, environmental factors (social background, teacher bias, school quality), and chance.
evaluation: Claims C70-C76 appropriately interpret the study's findings in context of broader understanding of educational achievement. The distinction between group and individual prediction (C71) is well-established, and the multifactorial nature of achievement (C73) is supported by cited literature. The inference about non-determinism (C72) follows from the distribution overlap data.

result: The authors conclude that while genetic personalization may work in medicine for some diseases, polygenic scores offer limited value for educational prediction beyond phenotypic data. However, genetic data remain useful for research on group-level differences, including teacher/school effectiveness, selection differences, social mobility, and Mendelian randomization studies.
evaluation: Claims C77-C84 appropriately contextualize findings and distinguish between individual prediction (not supported) and group-level research applications (supported by citations). The contrast with medical genetics (C77) is reasonable, and the cited examples of appropriate uses (C80-C83) demonstrate the authors understand the value of genetic data for different purposes.

result: Genetic studies focus heavily on European ancestry samples, and polygenic scores from these studies perform poorly in other ancestry groups. System-wide application could therefore lead to systematic prediction errors and inequalities in schooling.
evaluation: Claims C88-C90 correctly identify a major limitation of current polygenic scores with appropriate citations. The inference about potential inequalities (C90) logically follows from poor cross-ancestry performance (C89). This is an important consideration for policy applications.

result: Study limitations include: ALSPAC is not fully representative of UK population; polygenic scores were based on years of education (a more social measure) rather than exam scores, which may capture parental social position; alternative GWAS on test score changes might perform differently if genetic factors affect educational progress.
evaluation: Claims C91-C95 appropriately acknowledge study limitations. The representativeness issue (C91) is documented, the distinction between education measures (C92-C93) is valid, and the speculation about alternative approaches (C95) is reasonable. These limitations are important for interpreting generalizability.

result: Additional limitations: Current polygenic scores explain ~13% variance, and while future GWAS may improve this, heritability of educational attainment (~40%) fundamentally limits genetic prediction. Confounding biases (population stratification, assortative mating, dynastic effects) may inflate associations, masking social differences as genetic differences. Family data are needed to investigate these biases.
evaluation: Claims C96-C101 identify important methodological limitations with appropriate citations. The heritability constraint (C97-C98) is well-established, and the discussion of confounding biases (C99-C100) reflects current understanding in the field. The need for family data (C101) is a recognized methodological requirement.

result: Main conclusions: Currently available genetic scores are unlikely to provide more accurate predictions than easily measured phenotypes. Genetic data provide little additional information over readily available phenotypic data except when prior achievement is unavailable. The greatest value lies in research on etiology of group differences and sociogenomic analyses of inequalities.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 appropriately summarize the study's main conclusions, which are well-supported by the comprehensive analyses presented. The distinction between individual prediction utility (limited) and research value (substantial) is clearly demonstrated throughout the results.

result: Study sample consisted of children from ALSPAC cohort (14,541 initial pregnancies, 15,454 total, 14,901 alive at 1 year). After quality control, 7,988 had genetic data, and final analytical sample was 3,453 after listwise deletion. ALSPAC is largely representative of UK population but underrepresents some ethnic minorities, single parents, and renters.
evaluation: Claims C106-C112 accurately describe the study sample with specific numbers documented. The representativeness assessment (C110-C111) is appropriately qualified with citation. The substantial reduction from 7,988 to 3,453 due to missing data is clearly stated but raises questions about potential selection bias not fully addressed.

result: Genetic data were generated using Illumina HumanHap550 for children (9,115 participants, 500,527 SNPs passed QC) and Illumina human660W-quad for mothers (9,048 participants, 526,688 SNPs passed QC). Phased haplotypes were imputed to HRC reference panel (~31,000 phased genomes).
evaluation: Claims C113-C117 provide standard descriptions of genotyping and imputation procedures with specific platforms, sample sizes, and reference panels documented. These methods are appropriate and well-established for this type of genetic study.

result: Educational achievement measured using fine-graded point scores from UK National Pupil Database at ages 7, 11, 14, and 16. Two polygenic scores were generated using PRSice: GWAS sig PGS (1,271 genome-wide significant SNPs) and all SNP PGS (all genome-wide SNPs), based on Lee et al. 2018 GWAS with ALSPAC/23andMe removed (n=763,468).
evaluation: Claims C118-C123 clearly describe outcome measures and polygenic score construction. The use of NPD data is appropriate, and the exclusion of ALSPAC/23andMe from the GWAS (C121) properly avoids sample overlap. The two-score approach (genome-wide significant vs. all SNPs) is standard practice.

result: Covariates included sex, month of birth, and pupil characteristics available to schools (FSM, SEN, EFL status), plus parental education and socioeconomic position (CAMSIS). Statistical methods included regression with bootstrapped confidence intervals (1000 replications) for R² and ROC curve analysis for discrimination.
evaluation: Claims C124-C127 describe appropriate covariate selection and statistical methods. The choice of readily available school data is well-justified for the research question. Bootstrapping for confidence intervals and ROC analysis are appropriate methods for the analyses conducted.

result: Background on policy context: Polygenic scores have been promoted for genetically informed policy and personalized applications (medicine, education, dating). Personalized learning was adopted in England in 2004 but was not mandated and inconsistently implemented. Currently no policies rely on educational prediction, but calls are increasing for genetic data to personalize education.
evaluation: Claims C6-C11 provide appropriate policy context with citations. These claims accurately characterize the landscape of proposals for genetic applications in education and the history of personalized learning policy, setting up the motivation for the study.

result: Background on polygenic scores and prediction: Education polygenic scores associate with many environmental factors (gene-environment correlation). Theoretical work shows polygenic scores are more predictive when heritability is higher and (for binary outcomes) prevalence is higher. Phenotypic measures (sex, birth month, prior achievement, parental education/SES) predict achievement, but few studies have examined polygenic prediction conditional on readily available phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C12-C20 provide appropriate scientific background with citations. The discussion of gene-environment correlation (C12-C14) and theoretical prediction limits (C16-C17) is accurate. The identification of the research gap (C20) appropriately motivates the study.

result: The findings are consistent with the only other comparable study (Lee et al., 2018), which found parental education explained more variance (18-21.3%) than polygenic scores (10.6-12.7%) in two US samples.
evaluation: Claim C60 appropriately contextualizes findings with the only comparable prior study. The consistency across studies strengthens confidence in the results, though the limited number of comparable studies is notable.

result: Teachers have access to wide-ranging non-genetic information from daily interactions (student responses, life events, physical/mental health) used to inform teaching. To the extent this captures genotypic information through phenotypic expression, it is unclear what novel information genotype would offer.
evaluation: Claims C85-C87 make a logical argument about the redundancy of genetic information when phenotype is already observed. This reasoning is sound and supported by the empirical finding that polygenic scores add little beyond phenotypic measures. However, this assumes complete phenotypic expression, which may not always hold.
